source.title: Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment: Balancing Transfer and Cultural Erasure in Multilingual LLMs
source.authors: HyoJung Han; Sweta Agrawal; Eleftheria Briakou

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-language representation geometry and finds convergence depends on the inputs and layer: universal-question representations merge earlier, while culturally specific inputs remain more separable. This refines a broad convergence claim rather than testing convergence with model scale.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 and Section 4.4 report qualitative PCA results on language representations across layers and datasets. Accuracy changes on GMMLU and BLEND evaluate task performance, not representation similarity, so they are not included as rows. The study also reports steering-vector angles and steering effects, which do not directly measure the claim's cross-language representation convergence. Results cited from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study does not test the claim. Every version concerns representations of different models (or seeds, or modalities) converging. This study instead compares representations of different languages inside one model, Gemma3 12B. The convergence it reports is largely induced on purpose by cross-lingual alignment training (MIST, CLO, MIDALIGN), whose objectives target cross-language alignment; MIDALIGN's loss directly maximises middle-layer similarity. Its evidence is qualitative PCA plots, with no cross-model similarity measure. This is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that cross-lingual alignment methods consistently improve universal knowledge transfer (GMMLU) at the cost of cultural localization (BLEND) across six languages. Transfer and localization are best steered at different layers (20 vs 28), and layer-specific Surgical Steering partly recovers cultural knowledge. Some cultural nuance is irretrievably lost, most for strongly aligned models.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines multilingual alignment methods and layer-wise PCA representations within Gemma3 12B; it does not reproduce a scale-convergence experiment or compare independently trained, architecturally distinct models.
record.method_sensitivity: Representation convergence differs between GMMLU and BLEND inputs and across layers: middle-layer merging is reported for GMMLU, while BLEND representations remain largely separable there and show alignment emerging deeper in the model.

fits_no_version.finding: Within Gemma3 12B, hidden states for parallel inputs in different languages overlap in middle layers (16-32) on universal GMMLU questions but stay largely separable on culture-specific BLEND questions. Cross-lingual alignment training (MIST, CLO, MIDALIGN) tightens clustering, especially at deeper layers such as layer 28. The evidence is qualitative PCA plots.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a multilingual LLM, cross-language representation convergence depends on layer and on whether the content is universal or culture-specific.

record.problems: Representation results are qualitative PCA projections without reported numerical similarity scores or uncertainty. The experiments use a single model family and size, and do not test scale, independent seeds, or alternative similarity metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant PCA condition rows were left out. Task-accuracy results and steering-vector analyses were omitted because they do not directly measure the cross-language representation similarity specified by the claim.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep and no comparison of independently trained models.
No vision-language models and no image-caption alignment.
No mapping, stitching or relative representations between models.
No analysis of features or circuits recurring across models.
No cross-model similarity measure, so no test of dependence on metric, neighbour settings or inputs. Its input and layer dependence concerns within-model cross-language geometry.
No cross-model alignment level, plateau, or test of shared training data as the cause of alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5 classification treated cross-lingual, within-model convergence as if it were the claim's cross-model convergence. Alignment here is an engineered training target, not convergence arising independently. Gemma3 12B only; PCA evidence is qualitative.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, and no comparison of independently trained models differing in architecture, objective, or data.
No vision-language model comparison or image-caption paired-data alignment.
No comparison across random seeds or analysis of shared features or subspaces across seed-trained networks.
No mapping between models, stitching, relative-representation method, or unpaired mapping.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.
Tests input dataset and layer dependence using qualitative PCA projections. It does not compare alternative similarity metrics or neighbour settings, or report out-of-distribution results.

Shows incomplete, dataset- and layer-dependent convergence. It does not test whether convergence plateaus, or whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: MIST
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative PCA comparison of hidden representations across languages
rows.value: CLA methods merge language representations in the middle layers on GMMLU.
rows.note: The paper describes this as the intended alignment effect; the result is qualitative, not a numerical similarity score.
rows.check: Measures cross-language clustering within one model after training aimed at alignment. That is neither cross-model convergence nor its metric or data dependence. The state is not determinable against any version.

rows.subject: MIST
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative PCA comparison of hidden representations across languages
rows.value: CLA methods induce stronger convergence in deeper layers, with layer 28 given as an example.
rows.note: Qualitative finding; no numerical distance is reported.
rows.check: Within-model cross-language geometry after purpose-built alignment training; not a version's construct. Qualitative PCA only.

rows.subject: MIST
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative PCA comparison of hidden representations across languages
rows.value: Language representations remain largely separable in the middle layers on BLEND.
rows.note: The paper says this separation persists even in the most stringently aligned models.
rows.check: Within-model cross-language separability on BLEND. It does not bear on convergence between independently trained models.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GMMLU versus BLEND inputs and middle versus deep layers
reader_labels.reason: The reported PCA pattern changes with both dataset and layer: GMMLU representations merge in middle layers, while BLEND representations remain separated there and show only emerging alignment deeper in the model (r1-r12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BLEND culturally specific inputs, especially middle layers
reader_labels.reason: The aligned models retain substantial cross-language separation on BLEND, with alignment only beginning to appear in deeper layers (r3-r4, r7-r8, r11-r12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: On GMMLU, the authors report merged representations in middle layers and stronger convergence deeper in the model, so the degree of partial convergence depends on the input type (r1-r2, r5-r6, r9-r10).
